demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
I remind myself it could have been worse
I dwell on what I have done wrong

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I feel isolated and set apart from others
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only markedly high-risk/impulsive strategy and is poorly supported by the rest of the selected nodes. The other strategies are comparatively cognitive/obsessional (mental rituals, downward comparison), and the threat/memory/appraisal items do not show the broader dysregulation, dissociation, or severe affective overload that would make this combination clinically cohesive.

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Pain recall implies the patient was physically injured in the traumatic event. That is hard to reconcile with the trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another' unless she was also injured, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. The rest of the memory items emphasize fragmented retrieval and sensory reliving, but not a personally injured trauma narrative.

vignette:
Amina is a 47-year-old married architect who came to treatment months after an accident in which she seriously injured another person. She speaks about the event in a halting way, as if the memory both presses in on her and slips away when she tries to hold it directly. The accident happened at the end of a long workday, when she was driving home after leaving a construction meeting. She had been thinking about unfinished drawings and the next morning's presentation when, in a moment she still revisits relentlessly, she failed to respond in time and struck a pedestrian in a crosswalk. What remains with her most sharply is not a coherent narrative she can tell from beginning to end, but fragments that arrive with force: the sound of the impact, other people shouting, the high, confused noise in the street, and the taste in her mouth in those first seconds afterward, metallic and sour, as if panic itself had a flavor. When the memory returns, she hears those sounds again in her head with alarming clarity. At the same time, if she tries to deliberately sit down and recount exactly what happened, she often says her mind goes blank around the crucial moments, which she experiences as both frightening and incriminating.

In the immediate aftermath, Amina became preoccupied with what she had done wrong. She goes over tiny details repeatedly-the route she chose, the timing of her departure, whether she should have stayed later at the office, whether another person would have been more alert, more careful, more deserving of trust. She has come to believe that somebody else would not have gotten into this situation. This idea has lodged itself deeply enough that she no longer describes the accident as something terrible that happened, but as evidence about the kind of person she is. When she looks at herself now, she feels estranged: the woman who once managed complex projects, coordinated teams, and took pride in precision feels unrecognisable to her. She says that before the accident she knew how to move through the world with confidence; now she feels like someone diminished and morally suspect.

Over the following weeks, her days narrowed around habits that made sense to her in the moment, even as they consumed more of her attention. She began performing mental rituals, silent phrases and private sequences of thought, especially before driving, before her husband left the house, or before she sent colleagues to job sites. If she completed them properly, she felt she was less likely to let another catastrophe happen. If she was interrupted, she started over. Alongside this, she tried to steady herself by reminding herself it could have been worse, that the person had survived, that no one died. But even this relief never lasted; it quickly turned back into long spells of dwelling on what she should have done differently.

Her work as an architect has become one of the places where the accident feels closest. On construction sites, ordinary noises make her body react before she can think: a dropped metal tool, a reversing truck beep, a shouted warning across scaffolding. She jumps violently at sounds that would once have blended into the workday. More than once she has turned abruptly toward a harmless noise with the certainty that something terrible is about to happen. In design meetings she loses track of conversations and finds herself staring at plans without taking in the details, unsettled by how hard it has become to concentrate in a profession that depends on sustained attention. She now avoids visiting some sites unless absolutely necessary, delegating tasks she once handled herself. Colleagues have noticed she is less decisive, and this has embarrassed her, reinforcing her sense that she is no longer the person they knew.

At home, Amina feels separate even from her husband. She does not describe conflict so much as distance. Around other people she feels marked by what happened, as if she occupies a different moral category from everyone else. When friends talk casually about traffic, errands, or being tired after work, she feels herself withdraw. She assumes they could not understand how a single ordinary drive could divide a life into before and after. What frightens her most is not only that the sensory fragments still break through-the sounds in her head, the sudden return of that taste-but that these moments seem to confirm she is still dangerous, still capable of ruining a life through one lapse.

She sought help after a recent site visit where a sudden clang of steel made her jolt so hard she dropped her tablet and had to step away, unable to follow the conversation that came next. Sitting in her car afterward, she found herself unable to deliberately reconstruct the incident at the site, while the older accident flooded back in sounds and sensations. It left her shaken and ashamed. By the time she came to treatment, what she most wanted was not simply to feel calmer, but to understand whether she could live as herself again. What she fears is that this altered, isolated version of her is permanent, and that if she lets her guard down, another irreversible mistake will happen.
